problemText: When a community chooses where to build a new library, what two types of facts must they check about a candidate site?
choices: The site facts about what color the fence will be and the situation facts about the neighborhood's age.
The site facts about how many people live nearby and the situation facts about the building's color.
The situation facts about the ground itself and the site facts about nearby roads.
The site facts about the ground itself and the situation facts about what surrounds it.
hints: Think about the two questions from Unit 1: what is the ground like here, and what does this spot connect to?
Site and situation are the two categories you learned—one describes the ground, the other describes what is nearby.

problemText: A town is choosing between two lots for a new recreation center. Lot Pine is on high, dry ground with plenty of space, but it is far from most neighborhoods and no bus stops are near it. Lot Oak sits on wet, low ground that floods sometimes, but it is within walking distance of four neighborhoods. Which lot has the better site for a recreation center?
choices: Lot Pine, because high, dry ground is a strong site fact.
Lot Oak, because being close to neighborhoods is a strong site fact.
Lot Pine, because being far from neighborhoods makes a better site.
Lot Oak, because wet ground does not matter as much as good situation.
hints: Use the move-it test: which ground facts would travel with the lot if you picked it up and moved it?
Remember that site means the ground itself—not what is nearby. Does high, dry ground travel with the ground?

problemText: A student says, 'We should build the new swimming pool at the North Field because there is a big, empty space there and the ground is flat.' What is wrong with using only this reason to make the decision?
choices: The reason is wrong because a flat field is never a good site for a swimming pool and should be rejected on safety grounds.
The reason names only site facts and does not check the situation—whether students and families can actually reach the pool.
The reason fails to consider situation because it does not examine whether there are roads, parking, or transportation links to the North Field.
The reason is incomplete because it ignores situation factors such as whether the location is close enough for families and students to access.
hints: A good siting decision requires checking both site and situation. The student only talked about one. Which one did they leave out?
Flatness and empty space describe the ground itself. What else needs to be checked before the choice is complete?

problemText: Southridge is choosing between two lots for a new park. Lot Willow has firm, well-drained ground perfect for walking paths, sits two blocks from a school, and is across the street from a busy neighborhood where many families with children live. Lot Sterling has equally firm, well-drained ground and plenty of space, but it sits next to a highway on-ramp, is thirty minutes' walk from the nearest homes, and has no sidewalk connecting it to the surrounding streets. A parent argues that both lots have equally good sites, so either one would work equally well. Is the parent correct?
choices: Yes. Since both have firm, well-drained ground, the site facts are the same, so the parks would be equally good.
No. Lot Sterling has a better site because it is next to a highway, which makes it easier to reach.
No. Both lots have good sites, but Lot Willow has a much better situation, so it is the better overall choice.
No. Lot Willow has a better site because it is closer to the school.
hints: Identical site facts do not make two lots equally good choices. What else matters just as much?
One lot is close to families and neighborhoods; the other is isolated and far from homes. Does that difference belong to site or situation?

problemText: A community wants to build a new market hall. Three facts are offered as reasons to choose the Canal Street lot: (1) The ground is flat and solid and can support a large building; (2) The Canal Street lot is three blocks from the train station where shoppers arrive; (3) The market hall's roof will be made of recycled metal. Which fact or facts are genuine site or situation reasons that actually support this choice?
choices: All three facts, because they are all true statements that describe the Canal Street lot and its features.
Fact 1 only, because the roof material is about building design and construction, not about the location or ground itself.
Fact 3 only, because using recycled materials is always the most important factor when choosing where to build a market hall.
Facts 1 and 2 only, because they describe the ground and its connection to where shoppers come from.
hints: Remember: a justification must be grounded in a real fact about site or situation, not just any true fact about the place.
Check each fact with the move-it test and by asking: does this describe the ground itself, or what surrounds it? Does it matter for siting?

problemText: Two towns are arguing about which lot would be better for a shared youth center. Riverdale offers Lot M: rocky, uneven ground that would cost $50,000 to prepare for building, but the lot is one mile from Riverdale's town center and has five bus stops within a half-mile radius. Hillside offers Lot H: perfectly flat, easy-to-build-on ground, but it is two miles from Hillside's town center and has only one bus stop nearby—a half-hour walk away. An engineer claims that Lot M's cost to prepare ($50,000) makes it a weaker site than Lot H, so Lot H is the better choice for both towns. Is the engineer correct, and why or why not?
choices: No. The cost to prepare the ground is not a site or situation reason for siting—it is a cost fact. Lot M has a poor site but an excellent situation with five bus stops, while Lot H has a good site but a poor situation with only one distant bus stop.
Yes. The engineer is right because Lot H has ground that does not need expensive preparation, and that will save the towns money on construction, making it the more economical choice overall.
No. The cost fact makes Lot M the better choice automatically because any expense involved in preparing a site makes it unsuitable for a youth center and rules out Lot H as viable.
Yes. Because Lot M is rocky and costs more to prepare, it will never be as good a site as Lot H, even if bus stops nearby make it easier to reach for visitors and participants.
hints: A cost fact is different from a site fact. Cost is about money, not about whether the ground itself is suitable or what the lot connects to.
To choose between Lot M and Lot H, you must evaluate both the site and the situation separately. What makes Lot M's situation strong, and Lot H's situation weak?

problemText: On a map, a leg is one straight stretch of a route between two points. A route with two turns is made of how many legs?
choices: Three legs, because each turn creates a new segment
Two legs, because the route has two turns
One leg, because a route is a single path from start to finish
Four legs, one for each turn plus two more
hints: Count the straight stretches, not the turns themselves.
Each turn happens at the point where one leg ends and the next begins.

problemText: A map's scale bar is divided into four equal segments. Each segment is labeled to stand for 50 meters in the real world. A hiking path on the map spans exactly three of those segments. How far is the actual hiking path in meters?
choices: 50 meters
150 meters
100 meters
200 meters
hints: Multiply the number of segments the path spans by the distance each segment represents.
Do not add the number of segments to the distance per segment.

problemText: The Riverside Park Map shows a playground marked with a star and a pond marked with a circle. A path runs from the playground toward the bottom of the page to the pond. The map's compass rose shows its arrow labeled N pointing toward the top of the page. In which direction does the path from the playground to the pond run?
choices: North
East
South
West
hints: Look at where the compass rose shows north is pointing on this map.
If north is at the top, what direction is toward the bottom?

problemText: The Pinewood Trail Map shows a parking lot marked with a P and a waterfall marked with a W. Its legend shows a solid line for paved trail and a dashed line for dirt trail. A paved trail runs from the parking lot two scale-bar segments toward the right edge of the page to a junction. From the junction, a dirt trail continues one scale-bar segment toward the top of the page, ending at the waterfall. Each scale-bar segment stands for three miles. The map's compass rose shows its arrow labeled N pointing toward the top of the page. What are the two directions traveled, in order, and the total distance from the parking lot to the waterfall?
choices: Right, then up; total distance is five miles
East, then north; total distance is five miles
North, then east; total distance is nine miles
East, then north; total distance is nine miles
hints: Use the compass rose to find direction for each leg separately, not the page directions alone.
Multiply the number of segments in each leg by three miles, then add the two legs together.

problemText: The Twin Lakes Community Map shows a community center marked with a square and two possible locations for a new park, marked as Site A and Site B. A path to Site A runs two scale-bar segments toward the top of the page from the center. A path to Site B runs three scale-bar segments toward the bottom of the page from the center, then two more segments toward the left edge. Each segment stands for 200 yards. The legend confirms both are paved paths. Which site is closer to the community center, and by how many yards?
choices: Site A is closer by 400 yards
Site A is closer by 200 yards
Site B is closer by 200 yards
Site B is closer by 400 yards
hints: Calculate the total distance to each site separately before comparing.
Site B's distance requires adding two legs together first.

problemText: The Hillside Recreation Area Map shows a ranger station marked with an R, and two destinations: Overlook 1 marked with a triangle and Overlook 2 marked with a diamond. Its legend shows a solid line for main trail and a dashed line for side trail. From the ranger station, a main trail runs three scale-bar segments toward the bottom of the page to Overlook 1. From the ranger station, a side trail runs two scale-bar segments toward the top of the page to a rest shelter, then two scale-bar segments toward the right edge of the page to Overlook 2. Each segment is labeled to stand for 500 feet. A visitor uses the scale bar to check both routes but makes an error: she reads the compass rose as showing north toward the right edge of the page instead of toward the top of the page. How would this error change her conclusion about which overlook is closer, if at all?
choices: The error would make her think Overlook 1 is closer, even though Overlook 2 is actually closer by rotating her mental map and counting the segments in the new orientation
The error would not change her conclusion because segment distances do not depend on compass-rose orientation
The error would make her think Overlook 2 is closer by reversing the position of north, which would swap which route appears shorter when she counts segments again
The error would make both overlooks appear to be the same distance away because reorienting the compass rose would cause the two routes to seem equivalent in total length
hints: Decide whether changing the compass-rose reading affects how many segments each path spans.
Distances are determined by counting segments and multiplying by each segment's labeled value.

problemText: A river's course is the path the river follows as it flows across the land. Which statement best describes whether a river's course is fixed in place permanently or can change over time?
choices: A river's course is permanently fixed in place and can never shift to a different location no matter how much time passes.
A river's course can shift to different locations over a long stretch of time, even though it may look the same from one day to the next.
A river's course changes suddenly and dramatically whenever heavy rain or flooding occurs in a valley, moving noticeably in just a few hours.
A river's course only changes if a person digs a new channel and deliberately forces the water to follow it instead of its natural path.
hints: Remember that physical geography is not fixed, even when a place looks the same for a long time.
Think about whether a river must jump suddenly to a new location, or whether it can move gradually.

problemText: Two different maps of a coastline exist. The first map, made 50 years ago, marks the ocean's edge at a certain location. The second map, made today of the exact same stretch of coast, shows the water's edge sitting noticeably farther back from that original position. No storms, earthquakes, or other sudden events are recorded between the two maps. What most likely caused the change shown between these two maps?
choices: The coastline suddenly wore away in a single dramatic event that nobody recorded or noticed at the time.
The ocean level rose suddenly one time between the two map dates, pushing the water's edge back across the land in a single shift.
The coastline wore back gradually, a small amount at a time over the 50 years, too slowly to notice from day to day.
The second map must be incorrect because the coastline cannot change its position without a recorded sudden event or natural disaster.
hints: Look at what the maps do NOT tell you—there is no sudden event mentioned between them.
Gradual change adds up over many years without showing a jump from one day to the next.

problemText: A student observes a river flowing past a certain location on Tuesday. She returns to the exact same spot on Wednesday and sees the river running in exactly the same path. She repeats her observation every single day for two years, and each day the river looks the same as the day before. However, when she compares a detailed map of the river from two years ago with a map made today, the river's course is measurably different—it now follows a path several hundred meters away from where it was marked two years earlier. How is it possible for the river to look the same every day yet end up in a different location on the map?
choices: One of the two maps must be wrong, since the river cannot change its location without the student noticing it on one of her daily visits.
The river must have jumped to its new location on a day when the student did not visit, shifting position in a single sudden movement that occurred between two consecutive days she observed it.
The river's course did not actually change at all; the maps simply show it at different water levels during different seasons, so the apparent shift is only a result of seasonal variation in flow.
The river shifted gradually over the two years, a small amount at a time each day, so no single day looked different from the day before, but the tiny shifts added up to a measurable change.
hints: Gradual change means many small shifts that are too small to notice one at a time.
When small changes keep happening and adding up, even imperceptible daily changes can create a measurable difference over years.

problemText: A geography class compares two aerial photographs of a river taken exactly one year apart. In the first photograph, the river flows in a broad, looping bend across a flat plain. In the second photograph, taken a year later during an ordinary dry season with no unusual weather mentioned, the bend has shifted noticeably downstream. The class also finds an old written description of the same river from a surveyor's field notes taken 100 years ago, which describes the bend in yet another location, even farther downstream. Which explanation best fits all three pieces of evidence, and why does a sudden-change explanation not work well?
choices: The bend has been shifting gradually over the entire 100-year period, with small changes each year adding up to the measurable differences between all three observations, which fits the pattern of 'no sudden events mentioned' across the whole span.

The bend shifted gradually over most of the 100 years, but the one-year shift between the photographs had to be sudden and caused by an unrecorded flood, because large visible changes cannot happen gradually in just one year without a major weather event to drive them.

The bend must have jumped suddenly 100 years ago when the surveyor first measured it, then remained fixed in place for decades, then jumped suddenly again between the two recent photographs to explain why the written notes and current photographs show such different positions.

The surveyor's notes must be incorrect or fake because a bend cannot move more than a few dozen meters without a recorded major disaster, so a 100-year shift of several hundred meters contradicts the lack of any documented catastrophic event in that time period.
hints: Check whether a sudden-change explanation requires an event that is not mentioned in any of the evidence.
If the bend shifted the same small amount every year for 100 years, small yearly changes would add up to a large visible shift between the surveyor's notes and today.

problemText: Two photographs of the same rocky coastline are taken 10 years apart. The first photograph shows a rocky cliff face with a certain shape. The second photograph shows the cliff face now sitting about two meters farther back from the ocean than it was in the first photograph. The second photograph shows small cracks in the exposed rock face and a few loose rocks near the base, but no evidence of a recent collapse or debris pile. How do these clues point to gradual change rather than sudden change, and what would the clues look like if sudden change had caused the difference instead?
choices: Gradual change is shown because loose rocks appear and cracks form over time through weathering, while sudden change would show a fresh debris pile at the base from a single collapse event with recently broken rock still in place.

Gradual change is shown because the change happened over a long time span (10 years) and no single dramatic event is described; sudden change would mean a large difference appeared in a much shorter time, likely with fresh broken rock and debris piled at the cliff base from one specific event.

Gradual change is shown because the cliff moved exactly two meters, which is too small a distance to be caused by sudden change; sudden change only produces shifts larger than five meters and would show different physical evidence patterns.

Gradual change is shown because the cliff moved backward rather than downward, indicating erosion rather than collapse; sudden change would cause the cliff to collapse downward into a pile of rubble at its base instead.
hints: Compare the TIME SPAN and what physical EVIDENCE would be left by each type of change.
Sudden change from a single event would show fresh damage concentrated in one area; gradual wear leaves small cracks and loose rocks scattered over time.

problemText: A river maintenance crew has records of the river's path for the past 40 years. They observe the following pattern: between year 1 and year 20, the river's course shifted about 100 meters downstream. Between year 20 and year 40, it shifted another 120 meters downstream. Over those same 40 years, only two major floods are recorded—one in year 8 (when no visible change was noted) and one in year 35 (when surveyors reported the river in the same location as before the flood, just with higher water levels). The crew also discovers historical records from before year 1 showing the river 500 meters farther downstream than where it was in year 1. Using what you know about gradual and sudden change, which conclusion best explains the entire pattern and what it tells you about the river?
choices: The river must have shifted suddenly long before year 1 to reach its early position, then stayed mostly fixed in place until year 20, then shifted gradually across the remaining 20 years—a pattern suggesting that rivers in flat plains typically follow cycles of sudden displacement followed by long periods of stability.

The two recent floods must have caused the 220-meter shift across the 40 years, even though surveyors did not notice it immediately after each flood, which proves that sudden events can produce measurable changes that accumulate over months or years before becoming fully visible.

The river has been shifting gradually throughout the entire time span, so the 500-meter shift before year 1 and the 220-meter shift across the 40 years all fit a pattern of continuous small changes adding up; the recorded floods did not cause visible shifts because sudden events do not necessarily cause the large changes that gradual change does over long periods.

The 500-meter shift before year 1 proves that rivers can only change suddenly, so the gradual pattern seen in the past 40 years must be caused by many small unrecorded floods happening every few months throughout that time period, each contributing a tiny shift.
hints: Notice that the floods in the records did NOT produce measurable shifts, which tells you something about whether sudden events must cause visible changes.
Over 40 years, small yearly shifts adding up match the observed change, and 500 meters over a longer earlier period also fits a slow, steady pattern—no sudden jumping required.

problemText: A community planner is gathering information before deciding how to use a piece of land. What are the three kinds of facts a planner must collect about a piece of land?
choices: The distance to the nearest town, the temperature in summer, and the type of animals living there
How many people live near the land, what color the soil is, and whether trees grow there
The shape of the land, the water nearby and flood risk, and what resources the land offers
The price of the land, the names of the current owners, and how long it has been empty
hints: Think about the land itself, not about people or money.
The planner needs to know about flatness or steepness, flooding risk, and natural resources.

problemText: A planner must choose where to place a farm in a new community. One parcel is flat and has soil known to grow good crops, but it sits on a floodplain that floods every spring. Another parcel is steep and rocky with almost no soil, but it sits on high ground that never floods. Based on what a farm actually needs, which parcel is the better choice for the farm?
choices: The steep, rocky parcel, because high ground keeps crops dry and prevents water damage
The flat parcel, because the flooding will help water the crops and reduce irrigation costs
Neither parcel works for a farm, so the planner should buy a third piece of land elsewhere with better conditions
The flat parcel with good soil, because farms need flat land and fertile soil more than they need steep, rocky ground
hints: Remember the three things a farm needs: flat land, fertile soil, and a water source.
Flooding is a problem for some land uses, but not for farms—farms can get water elsewhere.

problemText: A town planner is deciding where to build new housing. Two parcels are available. Parcel X is flat, sits far from any stream, and has never flooded. Parcel Y is also flat, sits right next to a river, and has flooded three times in the past ten years. Which parcel should the planner choose for housing, and why?
choices: Parcel X, because housing needs to stay dry and never flood, and Parcel Y floods regularly
Parcel Y, because housing needs to be near water for drinking and daily use by residents
Parcel X, because it is farther away from roads and therefore quieter for residents living there
Parcel Y, because flat land is the most important fact for housing and Parcel Y is also flat
hints: Housing must be on land that stays dry and does not sit on a floodplain.
Being flat is necessary for housing, but so is staying dry—Parcel Y fails one of those needs.

problemText: A community planner is working with three pieces of land: Parcel 1 is flat, has fertile soil, and sits next to a year-round stream; Parcel 2 is steep and rocky with poor soil but sits on high ground next to a lake with a scenic view; Parcel 3 is flat but has sandy, poor soil and sits on a floodplain. The town needs to place a farm and a park. Parcel 1 is already spoken for as a farm. Which of the remaining two parcels should become the park, and what is the planning reason?
choices: Parcel 3, because flat land is easier for people to walk around in parks and reduces construction costs
Parcel 2, because steep, rocky land that does not suit farming or building can still become a park, and the view over the lake adds to its value
Parcel 2, because the scenic lake view attracts visitors who prefer mountains over farmland, making it more profitable for the town than other options
Parcel 3, because sandy, poor soil that cannot grow crops will still work fine for parks since parks do not need fertile land to function
hints: Parks can use land that farms and housing cannot—steep, rocky ground is fine for a park.
A planning reason points to a land, water, or resource fact about the parcel itself, not just what people might prefer.

problemText: A planner is reviewing a resident's proposal for the town's remaining land. The resident says: 'We should put housing on the rocky hillside because it would have a beautiful mountain view, and put the farm on the flat land near the road even though the soil is very poor.' The flat land is sandy and has never grown crops well. The rocky hillside sits high above any floodplain and has never flooded. What is wrong with this proposal, based on the land, water, and resource facts?
choices: The proposal is wrong because building houses on rocky ground costs too much money and the town does not have enough funds to pay for construction on difficult terrain
The proposal is wrong because rocky hillsides are always better suited to farming than flat land, and housing should only be placed in areas with the cheapest building costs

The proposal is wrong because a beautiful view is a preference, not a land fact, and the flat land's poor soil makes it unsuitable for farming, while the rocky hillside cannot support crops no matter where it sits
The proposal is wrong because rocky hillsides tend to flood more often than flat land, and floodplains are better for housing than for farms since water features protect homes
hints: A planning reason must point to a land, water, or resource fact, not to how much people would enjoy something.
A farm needs fertile soil—sandy soil that has never grown good crops elsewhere will not work for farming.

problemText: A community planner has four parcels to assign to four different uses: farm, housing, park, and road. Parcel A is flat, has fertile soil, and sits next to a steady stream. Parcel B is steep and rocky with no soil, sits on a hillside, and overlooks a pond. Parcel C is flat, has poor sandy soil, and sits on a floodplain. Parcel D is flat with poor soil but sits on high ground, and a busy existing road already runs along its edge connecting two neighborhoods. The town's main need is to improve the connection between the two neighborhoods. Using the land, water, and resource facts, explain which parcel should become the road, and why—then identify what land use each of the other three parcels should serve and name at least one land, water, or resource fact that supports each choice.
choices: Parcel A becomes the road because it is flat and has fertile soil, which makes construction easier. Parcel B becomes the housing because it sits high and overlooks water for scenic views. Parcel C becomes the farm because it is flat and accessible. Parcel D becomes the park because an existing road runs along its edge.

Parcel C becomes the road because it is flat and situated on the floodplain, which provides good drainage for vehicle traffic. Parcel A becomes the park because it is next to a steady stream and flat land works well for recreation. Parcel B becomes the housing because its high elevation prevents flooding. Parcel D should become the farm because it already has a road connection nearby for transporting crops.

Parcel B becomes the road because its rocky, steep ground provides a stable, durable base for vehicles to travel safely. Parcel A becomes the housing because it is flat and dry with water access. Parcel D becomes the farm because an existing road runs alongside it, making crop transport convenient. Parcel C should become the park because its floodplain location creates natural wetland habitats and seasonal water features for recreation.

Parcel D becomes the road because it already has a road running along it that connects two neighborhoods. Parcel A becomes the farm because it is flat, has fertile soil, and sits next to a steady stream. Parcel B becomes the park because its steep, rocky ground does not suit farming or housing. Parcel C remains available for future use because the floodplain makes it unsuitable for housing or farming.
hints: A road's primary need is to connect two places people already travel between, not to have flat or fertile land.
After placing the road, check each remaining parcel against what a farm, park, and housing need—some parcels fail more than one use because of their land, water, or resource facts.
